UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                           )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                )       Docket Nos. ER26-3380-000

                                REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                              FIRSTENERGY SERVICE COMPANY

        Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act ("FPA"), 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a), and Rule

713 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

("Commission" or "FERC"), 18 C.F.R. § 385.713 (2025), FirstEnergy Service Company

("FirstEnergy"),1 respectfully submits this Request for Rehearing of the Commission's order issued

on September 29, 2026 in the above-captioned proceedings, which accepted and suspended the

Reliability Backstop Procurement ("RBP") proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. ("PJM"),

established a paper hearing, and instituted a proceeding under FPA Section 206.2 This request is

timely because it is filed within thirty days of issuance of the September 29 Order.

        Rehearing is necessary because the September 29 Order, while correctly identifying several

of the defects in PJM's filing, does not fully reject PJM's proposal on the bases FirstEnergy raised

 in its Comments and Protest ("FirstEnergy Protest").3 Instead, the September 29 Order accepts the

filing, declares that every aspect of the RBP other than three discrete topics set for paper hearing

is just and reasonable,4 and then either summarily dismisses, or never addresses, the arguments

FirstEnergy raised on those very aspects. FPA Section 205 places the burden of proof on PJM, and

the Commission may accept PJM's proposal only if the record shows that PJM carried that burden.5

The Commission's obligation to engage in reasoned decision-making likewise requires that it

respond meaningfully to the objections raised before it.6 The September 29 Order falls short of

both requirements with respect to several of the issues raised in the FirstEnergy Protest.

       Specifically, the September 29 Order: (1) accepts PJM's levelized, MW-weighted average-

price framework without responding at all to FirstEnergy's showing that it permits sellers to "front

load" contract prices onto customers, a plainly unacceptable outcome when affordability concerns

are already at the forefront; (2) rejects FirstEnergy's protest that the procurement should prioritize

the resources that most effectively address reliability without engaging with the record evidence

FirstEnergy submitted; (3) finds PJM's supplier shortfall charges and seller collateral requirements

just and reasonable without addressing FirstEnergy's showing that customers are unprotected

against supplier underperformance after commercial operation; and (4) accepts PJM's demand

response gating criteria without resolving the ambiguity FirstEnergy identified as to whether

determinations is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and contrary to

law, and thus rehearing should be granted. Although FirstEnergy understands that PJM is planning

to submit a new filing pursuant to FPA Section 205, consistent with the Commission’s invitation

to do so, rehearing is still warranted to ensure these issues are preserved and appropriately decided

in the context of any new filing made by PJM.


I.     BACKGROUND

       Because the September 29 Order is the culmination of an expedited process that unfolded

over approximately nine months, several major events are relevant to this request. On January 16,

2026, the National Energy Dominance Council and the governors of all thirteen PJM states issued

the Statement of Principles, urging PJM to "[p]rovide 15-year price certainty for new capacity

resources" through a reliability backstop auction and to allocate the costs of new capacity to LSEs

with data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be curtailable. Shortly

thereafter the PJM Board announced its decision in the Critical Issue Fast Path ("CIFP") process

addressing large load additions, which included accelerating a backstop capacity procurement. In

April the PJM Board initiated a targeted CIFP process to develop the RBP. On June 30, 2026, the

PJM Members Committee voted on thirteen RBP proposals. Only one—sponsored by a coalition

of Electric Distributors and the Data Center Coalition ("Joint Proposal")—received the two-thirds

sector-weighted support needed for endorsement. PJM's own proposal did not. Then on July 14,

2026, PJM announced that the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction ("BRA") cleared short of the

PJM Region's reliability requirement. In response, on July 27, 2026, the PJM Board adopted PJM's

proposal, with three "targeted changes," rather than the Joint Proposal. PJM filed its RBP proposal




                                                 3
 ("July 31 RBP Proposal" or "Transmittal"), as supplemented, on August 14, 2026. The foregoing

events are more thoroughly described in the September 29 Order and the FirstEnergy Protest.7

       PJM describes the RBP as a one-time procurement of new capacity to address resource

adequacy challenges primarily driven by an influx of large loads.8 Under PJM's proposal,

PJMSettlement, Inc. would act as counterparty on behalf of LSEs to procure commitments from

new "RBP Resources" for fixed terms of up to fifteen years, starting no earlier than the 2028/2029

delivery year and ending no later than the 2042/2043 delivery year.9 PJM proposed to procure

capacity equal to the 6,831 MW shortfall in the 2028/2029 BRA (the "Initial RBP Target"),

adjusted downward for qualifying offset capacity and for load that qualifying Electric Distributors

elect to opt out of the RBP.10 PJM proposed to select offers on a pay-as-bid basis, subject to a

maximum willingness to pay $555/MW-day calculated as a MW-weighted average of the levelized

cost of all selected offers over all delivery years.11 PJM proposed to allocate the costs to Electric

Distributor zone/areas based on each zone/area's pro rata share of the difference between

forecasted Load Adjustments for the 2026/2027 and 2028/2029 delivery years, fixed for the

fifteen-year term, with further allocation to LSEs left to states and Relevant Electric Retail

Regulatory Authorities ("RERRAs").12 And PJM proposed to require LSEs to post collateral equal

to $1.5 million per committed RBP MW.13

        FirstEnergy agreed that new generation is needed, but demonstrated that fundamental

elements of PJM's proposal could not be approved consistent with FPA Section 205.14 FirstEnergy

showed, among other things, that: (1) PJM's levelized contract framework permits suppliers to

"front load" contract prices and creates unnecessary affordability risks; (2) the RBP should be

limited to the resources (namely, dispatchable resources) that most effectively address reliability

needs; (3) the Commission should direct PJM to strengthen supplier performance and credit

requirements; and (4) the Commission should direct PJM to clarify that its gating criteria require

binding contractual commitments for eligible demand response resources.15 FirstEnergy asked the

Commission to reject PJM's filing, institute an FPA Section 206 proceeding, and establish

settlement procedures, following the model the Commission used when PJM first proposed the

Reliability Pricing Model ("RPM").16

       The September 29 Order did not reject the filing. It accepted PJM's proposed tariff

revisions and Reliability Assurance Agreement ("RAA") revisions for filing, suspended them for

five months to become effective February 28, 2027, subject to refund, and established paper

hearing procedures limited to three topics: cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit rules, and

LSE collateral requirements.17 The September 29 Order found that "the other aspects of PJM's

RBP proposal are just and reasonable,"18 instituted a proceeding in Docket No. EL26-108-000 on

the preliminary finding that PJM's existing Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable,19 anticipated

II.     STATEMENT OF ISSUES AND SPECIFICATIONS OF ERROR

        The following Statement of Issues and Specifications of Error is provided pursuant to Rule

713(c)(1) and Rule 713(c)(2), 18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(1)-(2).

        A.      The September 29 Order is arbitrary and capricious, fails to engage in reasoned
                decision-making, and is unsupported by substantial evidence because it accepts
                PJM's levelized, MW-weighted average maximum willingness to pay $555/MW-
                day without responding to FirstEnergy's showing that the framework permits sellers
                to front-load contract prices into the initial delivery years, exposing customers to
                unnecessary affordability risk. 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a); FCC v. Prometheus Radio
                Project, 592 U.S. 414 (2021); Me. Pub. Utils. Comm'n v. FERC, 520 F.3d 464 (D.C.
                Cir. 2008); NorthWestern Corp. v. FERC, 884 F.3d 1176 (D.C. Cir. 2018).

        B.      The September 29 Order is arbitrary and capricious, fails to engage in reasoned
                decision-making, and is unsupported by substantial evidence because it finds PJM's
                resource eligibility and selection rules just and reasonable without considering the
                record evidence FirstEnergy presented that firm, dispatchable resources provide the
                essential reliability services needed to address the reliability shortfall that is the

III.    ARGUMENT

       A.      The Commission Erred in Accepting PJM's Levelized Average-Price
               Framework Without Responding to FirstEnergy's Showing That It Permits
               Front-Loaded Contract Prices.

       PJM proposes that the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP Sell Offers not

exceed $555/MW-day on a MW-weighted average basis over all delivery years of the RBP.24 PJM

characterizes this as a "budget approach" that "allows for potentially fluctuating offers across the

15 delivery years of the RBP term," and contends that prices above $555/MW-day "in some




24
       September 29 Order at P 55; FirstEnergy Protest at 10 n.28 (citing July 31 RBP Proposal at 61-64;
Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, § 18.5(f)).


                                                   7
 delivery years may nevertheless be appropriate."25 Levelized cost is calculated using a discount

rate equal to a 9.5% after-tax weighted average cost of capital.26

       FirstEnergy explained that the predictable consequence of this flexibility is that sellers will

front-load their costs into the initial years of their contracts. A seller could, for example, offer

$1,000/MW-day for the first several years of the contract and balance that out with sub-market

prices in the later years, forcing customers to bear extremely large increases in capacity costs in

the initial delivery years—during a period of acute concern, including among members of this

Commission, about affordability.27 FirstEnergy further demonstrated that a levelized structure that

authorizes the front loading of payments is not needed: the Statement of Principles calls for fifteen-

year price certainty; significant new generation is being built by vertically integrated utilities with

straight-line, fixed-value cost recovery; and experience under PURPA shows that non-incumbent

investors are generally willing to build new generation on a straight-line, fixed-value basis.28

       The September 29 Order does not respond to this argument. The Commission instead finds

that a maximum willingness to pay "set at the MW-weighted average of the levelized procurement

cost over the RBP commitment term reasonably balances the need to expeditiously procure

capacity . . . with ensuring that the average procurement price does not exceed load's maximum

willingness to pay," and that $555/MW-day is a reasonable proxy for load's maximum willingness

to pay.29 Those findings address the average level of the cap, but not the temporal distribution of

payments that the averaging methodology permits. That temporal distribution—and the resulting

also accepts PJM's pay-as-bid structure while acknowledging that sellers in a pay-as-bid auction

are "less likely to offer near their marginal costs."30 The combination of pay-as-bid pricing and an

average-only constraint is precisely what invites strategic front-loading, yet the September 29

Order does not consider that interaction.

       The risk is compounded by other features of the proposal the September 29 Order accepted.

Under PJM's proposal, a resource that does not reach commercial operation and provide any RBP

UCAP MW for three consecutive delivery years has its commitment rescinded for the remainder

of the term.31 A resource that collects front-loaded payments and then ceases performance before

the later, lower-priced years leaves customers having paid a premium without receiving the

offsetting discount. Intervenors identified this very risk, noting that ratepayers could pay more

than $555/MW-day if any resource fails to materialize or ceases operation prior to the end of the

RBP term.32 The September 29 Order does not address it. Because the Commission accepted the

levelized framework without responding to FirstEnergy's showing, its determination is arbitrary

and capricious. The Commission should grant rehearing and reject the levelized framework or, in

the alternative, require that RBP offers be priced on a straight-line, fixed-value basis or subject to

an annual price cap.

        B.      The Commission Erred in Finding PJM's Resource Eligibility and Selection
               Rules Just and Reasonable Without Considering FirstEnergy's Evidence
               Regarding the Reliability Value of Dispatchable Resources.

       PJM justifies the RBP as an extraordinary measure necessary to address the approximately

6,831 MW capacity shortfall identified in the 2028/2029 BRA and to preserve resource adequacy

in the PJM Region.33          FirstEnergy demonstrated that, because the stated purpose of the

procurement is to address a reliability need, the Commission should ensure that it prioritizes

resources that provide firm and dependable capacity.34 FirstEnergy supported that showing with

record evidence from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ("NERC"), which has

identified that conventional generators provide much of the essential reliability services that

support reliable operation of the grid; that wind and solar resources lack the spinning mass and

traditional excitation systems that provide voltage control and stability; and that dispatchable

generators provide system inertia, dynamic reactive support, and frequency response for stable

grid operation.35 FirstEnergy further showed that PJM's selection process is designed to select the

"least-cost set of resources" without sufficient consideration of the relative reliability value of

different resource types.36

       The September 29 Order finds PJM's eligibility requirements and selection process just and

reasonable.37 It disposes of the argument that the selection process should value dispatchable

generation's reliability attributes in a single sentence, stating that the Commission does "not find

such additional valuation metrics to be necessary for PJM's proposal to be just and reasonable"

attributes.38 The September 29 Order acknowledges FirstEnergy's position in a footnote and does

not discuss the NERC evidence on which that position rests.39 Nor does the September 29 Order

explain how ELCC accreditation—a measure of a resource's contribution to resource adequacy—

accounts for the inertia, dynamic reactive support, frequency response, and voltage control that

NERC identified as needed for reliability. The September 29 Order similarly dismisses the

concern that four-hour storage and stand-alone solar resources are poorly matched to around-the-

clock data center demand on grounds that the same energy must-offer requirements apply to RBP

Resources as to other resources of their type,40 which does not answer whether a fifteen-year,

customer-funded procurement justified on reliability grounds should prioritize resources that

provide the greatest reliability value. The September 29 Order’s conclusory statement ignores the

record evidence and thus is not reasoned decision-making.

       The Commission should grant rehearing and require PJM to demonstrate that the RBP

framework appropriately prioritizes firm and dependable capacity resources.41 In this era of acute

affordability concerns, no better exemplified than by the inflated capacity costs that ratepayers in

PJM are already forced to shoulder even before implementation of an RBP, it is inappropriate to

require customers to pay even more for resources that are unable to provide the dispatchability and

other operational characteristics that are essential to meeting the needs of the moment. Data center

and other large load customers overwhelmingly need and desire on-demand service. The resources

       C.       The Commission Erred in Finding PJM's Supplier Performance and Credit
                Provisions Just and Reasonable Without Addressing the Risk of Post-
                Commercial Operation Underperformance.

       FirstEnergy demonstrated that the Commission should ensure that customers are

adequately protected against supplier non-performance over the full fifteen-year commitment

term.42 PJM's proposed protections are directed primarily toward construction risk and the risk

that a resource fails to come online in the first instance: PJM proposes an RBP UCAP MW shortfall

charge when a committed resource fails to achieve commercial operation, and rescission of the

commitment if the resource fails to provide any committed RBP UCAP MW after three

consecutive delivery years.43 As FirstEnergy showed, those provisions do not protect customers

against the possibility that a resource satisfies its initial commercial operation obligations and then

underperforms during the balance of its commitment term—even though LSEs, and ultimately

retail customers, remain responsible for funding the commitment throughout that term.44

FirstEnergy further showed that the asymmetry is particularly striking because PJM proposes

substantial, and unnecessary, collateral requirements to protect suppliers against the risk of

customer non-payment, and asked the Commission to require enhanced performance assurance

requirements, ongoing credit support, or other mechanisms ensuring that resources receiving long-

term RBP commitments remain accountable to customers throughout the commitment period.45

        The September 29 Order does not address FirstEnergy’s argument. The Commission

instead finds PJM's shortfall charges just and reasonable because they "will deter speculative

resources from seeking to participate in the RBP auction without creating an undue barrier to

entry," and because those penalties, together with the pay-as-bid approach and up to fifteen years

of revenue certainty, "will incentivize developers of RBP Resources to deliver their RBP UCAP

MW."46 That reasoning confirms FirstEnergy's point rather than answering it: the shortfall charge,

by PJM's design, applies only when a committed RBP Resource "has not reached commercial

operation," and "[o]nce an RBP Resource has achieved commercial operation, . . . RBP UCAP

29 Order finds that seller collateral requirement just and reasonable because it reduces risks

"associated with non-payment of RBP Shortfall Charges,"49 but offers no explanation of what

protects customers after commercial operation, when shortfall charges no longer apply.

       D.       The Commission Erred in Accepting PJM's Demand Response Gating
                Criteria Without Resolving Whether Eligible Demand Response Must Be
                Supported by Binding Contractual Commitments.

       FirstEnergy demonstrated that PJM's proposed gating criteria for demand response

resources appear to require only a contract or agreement evidencing a "plan or evidence of

deployed enabling infrastructure," not a contract or agreement demonstrating a clear and binding

commitment to provide the MWs sold into the RBP.59 If demand response resources may satisfy

the gating criteria based merely on a "plan," rather than a binding commitment for the underlying

demand response capability, the proposal risks treating speculative resources as equivalent to

committed resources—a result that would defeat the purpose of the RBP and require data centers

to pay for capacity that has not genuinely been procured.60 FirstEnergy therefore asked the

Commission to require PJM to clarify that eligible demand response resources must be supported

by binding contractual commitments.61

       The September 29 Order summarizes FirstEnergy's argument,62 but does not resolve it.

The Commission finds PJM's gating criteria just and reasonable because they purportedly "will

help to deter speculative resources from bidding into the RBP auction and ensure that the selected

RBP Resources are those most likely to go into service."63 The September 29 Order's analysis of

September 29 Order does not resolve either request.

        The September 29 Order's rationale underscores why rehearing or clarification is required.

The Commission accepted the gating criteria precisely because the criteria are intended to deter

speculative resources and ensure that selected resources are those most likely to go into service.67

A criterion that can be satisfied by a mere plan for the infrastructure necessary to deliver the offered

load reduction does not serve that purpose, and the September 29 Order does not explain how it

does. Because the September 29 Order accepts the criteria without resolving an ambiguity

squarely raised in the record, it fails to engage in reasoned decision-making. The Commission

should grant rehearing or, in the alternative, clarify that Demand Resources and DER Capacity

IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth herein, FirstEnergy respectfully requests that the Commission

grant rehearing of the September 29 Order on the issues specified above. Specifically, the

Commission should reject PJM's RBP filing, proceed under the Section 206 proceeding it has

instituted in Docket No. EL26-108-000, and establish settlement procedures. In the alternative,

and at a minimum, the Commission should: (1) reject PJM's levelized average-price framework;

(2) direct PJM to strengthen supplier performance assurance and credit requirements for the full

commitment term and to clarify that eligible demand response resources must be supported by

binding contractual commitments; (3) reject PJM’s shortfall charge proposal because it fails to

ensure that customers are adequately protected against supplier non-performance over the full

fifteen-year commitment term; (4) vacate its preliminary findings that PJM's eligibility

requirements and selection process are just and reasonable; and (5) expand the scope of the paper

hearing to encompass the arguments identified herein that the September 29 Order did not address.
